item.title: Apple iPhone Duo joins the foldable phone market: do Chinese brands still have the edge?
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: Apple has finally entered the foldable smartphone market. This week, Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, with a starting price of $1,999. The device features a 7.6-inch inner display when unfolded and a 5.4-inch outer display when folded. It is powered by the A20 Pro chip, supports split-screen multitasking and Apple Pencil, […]
item.content:encoded:
Apple has finally entered the foldable smartphone market. This week, Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, with a starting price of $1,999. The device features a 7.6-inch inner display when unfolded and a 5.4-inch outer display when folded.

It is powered by the A20 Pro chip, supports split-screen multitasking and Apple Pencil, and offers up to 2TB of storage. Apple also highlighted a new precision hinge, a reduced-crease design, and an iOS experience optimized specifically for the foldable form factor.

Apple’s promotional video also reveals how the company wants consumers to think about the foldable form factor. Through a series of fast and highly stylized scene transitions, the iPhone Duo moves between different scenarios as it folds and unfolds, making the change in form feel almost seamless.

The focus is not simply on the mechanical act of folding the phone, but on how that change can alter the user’s interaction with the device. In that sense, Apple is presenting the foldable iPhone less as a new type of hardware and more as a phone that can adapt its form to different situations.

For Apple, the launch represents one of the biggest changes to the iPhone’s form factor in more than a decade. But in China, Apple is not entering an empty market.

Chinese smartphone makers including Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo have been competing in the foldable segment for years. They have released multiple generations of foldable phones while continuously working to reduce weight and thickness and improve hinges, display creases, battery life, and software optimization for larger screens.

As Apple begins to explore what a foldable iPhone should look like, Chinese manufacturers are already asking what the next generation of foldable phones should look like.

Apple takes a relatively mature approach

The iPhone Duo does not take the most aggressive approach. It adopts the book-style horizontal fold that has become one of the more established designs in the market. Its 7.6-inch inner display offers a screen size close to that of a small tablet when unfolded, while the 5.4-inch outer display is designed for everyday smartphone use. Apple says the two displays use consistent proportions to ensure that content can transition smoothly between the folded and unfolded states.

This design has already gone through several generations of development in China. For example, Huawei’s Mate X7 features an 8-inch inner display and a 6.49-inch outer display. It is about 9.5mm thick when folded and weighs around 235 grams.

Oppo’s Find N6 features an 8.12-inch inner display and a 6.62-inch outer display, measuring about 8.93mm thick when folded and weighing around 225 grams. The Vivo X Fold6 features an 8.02-inch inner display and a 6.51-inch outer display, with a weight starting at around 228 grams.

By comparison, the iPhone Duo weighs around 254 grams and measures 11.3mm thick when folded, making it heavier and thicker than the three Chinese foldable phones mentioned above.

This points to an interesting reality: when Apple is making its first foldable phone, Chinese manufacturers have moved the competition beyond whether a phone can fold to whether a foldable can be as thin and light as a conventional smartphone.

Still, weight alone does not determine the overall user experience. Apple has its own advantages in structural design, hinges, and display technology. The company also says the Duo is the thinnest iPhone ever when unfolded (5.2mm thick) and uses a new hinge and display design to reduce the visibility of the crease.

But in terms of hardware iteration, Chinese smartphone makers clearly have more experience with foldable devices.

The real competition may be software

However, looking only at hardware specifications could underestimate the significance of Apple’s entry. The biggest challenge for foldable phones has never been just the hinge or the display. It is how to make the larger screen genuinely useful.

The iPhone Duo introduces split-screen multitasking for its larger display and supports Apple Pencil. Apple is hoping that users will be able to handle multiple tasks when the phone is unfolded, rather than simply seeing an enlarged version of the standard iPhone interface.

Chinese manufacturers are exploring the same direction. The Vivo X Fold6 features an 8.02-inch inner display and supports multitasking on the larger screen. Oppo’s Find N6 goes further by positioning itself as a Pocket AI Workstation, supporting multiple apps running simultaneously, adjustable windows, and desktop-style multitasking features such as Split View.

Huawei has also added features such as split-screen translation, split-screen navigation, AI call summaries, AI call translation, and multi-device collaboration to the Mate XT 2, turning its tri-fold design into more than just a larger display and positioning it as an AI and productivity tool.

Therefore, the real competition Apple faces is not simply who has the larger screen, but who can actually change the way consumers use their phones.

Apple has an ecosystem advantage Chinese brands cannot easily replicate

Apple also has an advantage that Chinese smartphone makers will find difficult to replicate: a tightly integrated hardware and software ecosystem. The A20 Pro chip, iOS, Apple Pencil, and integration across the iPhone, iPad, and Mac could all become important selling points for the foldable iPhone.

For users who already own an iPhone, Mac, or iPad, buying a foldable iPhone is not simply about purchasing another smartphone. It could introduce a new way of interacting with their existing devices. This also helps explain why Apple can afford to enter the foldable market years after other manufacturers.

It does not need to prove that there is demand for foldable phones. Chinese manufacturers, along with Samsung and others, have already helped establish the category. What Apple needs to prove is whether a foldable can become the next iPhone, rather than simply a more expensive iPhone.

Apple is the newcomer, but Chinese brands face new challenges

Apple’s entry into the foldable market cuts both ways. For Chinese manufacturers, Apple represents a new competitor. With its strong brand, massive user base, and mature developer ecosystem, Apple could help push foldable phones further into the mainstream if the foldable iPhone gains traction.

At the same time, Apple’s entry could also validate years of experimentation by Chinese manufacturers. By the time Apple entered the foldable market, Huawei was already exploring tri-fold designs, Oppo was continuing to reduce the weight and visibility of creases on its foldables, and Vivo was exploring AI and productivity features for large screens.

So this is not simply a competition between Apple and Chinese smartphone brands. More accurately, it is a collision between two different product approaches: Apple is looking to redefine the foldable experience through its mature ecosystem and software, while Chinese manufacturers are drawing on years of hardware iteration to explore how much further foldable phones can go.

Apple may have entered the foldable race late, but it has changed the question for everyone else. For Chinese smartphone makers, the challenge is no longer simply to make foldables thinner, lighter, or more advanced. It is to keep finding new ways to make the form factor useful — and convince consumers that a foldable phone can be more than just a phone that folds.

item.title: China targets 9,800 EFLOPS of intelligent computing capacity by 2030
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has set a target of 9,800 EFLOPS of intelligent computing capacity by 2030 under its 15th Five-Year Plan for the information and communications industry. The plan calls for RMB 3.8 trillion in information infrastructure investment from 2026 to 2030 and the construction of computing clusters with 10,000 or […]
item.content:encoded:
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has set a target of 9,800 EFLOPS of intelligent computing capacity by 2030 under its 15th Five-Year Plan for the information and communications industry.

The plan calls for RMB 3.8 trillion in information infrastructure investment from 2026 to 2030 and the construction of computing clusters with 10,000 or more accelerator cards, including some with 100,000 or more cards. China’s intelligent computing capacity stood at 2,185 EFLOPS at the end of June, up 177% year on year. The country had 52 facilities each containing more than 10,000 accelerators. [TechNode reporting]

The network connects several venues in the West Bund area and currently includes nearly 20 restaurant chains, with more than 40 expected by the end of the year. Meituan […]
item.content:encoded:
Meituan has opened a low-altitude delivery network in Shanghai’s West Bund and launched China’s first dedicated drone-delivery route for a restaurant brand in partnership with McDonald’s.

The network connects several venues in the West Bund area and currently includes nearly 20 restaurant chains, with more than 40 expected by the end of the year. Meituan says the fastest deliveries can arrive in 10 minutes, using its fourth-generation M-Drone 4L Winch, M-Port 3 drone ports and M-DaaS 3 scheduling system. [NBD, in Chinese]

item.title: Beyond Oil and Gas: How Kazakhstan Wants to Become a Gateway for Chinese Capital and Technology
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: For many Chinese investors, Kazakhstan and Central Asia have long been associated with natural resources—oil, gas, mining and commodities. Zhanbolat Kakishev, Chief Product Officer of the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), believes that perception is beginning to change. “Traditionally, China always looked into the advanced economies—Europe, America, Australia, Canada—and tried to do business and build […]
item.content:encoded:
For many Chinese investors, Kazakhstan and Central Asia have long been associated with natural resources—oil, gas, mining and commodities.

Zhanbolat Kakishev, Chief Product Officer of the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), believes that perception is beginning to change.

“Traditionally, China always looked into the advanced economies—Europe, America, Australia, Canada—and tried to do business and build production there because they would like to be closer to the international customer,” Kakishev told TechNode in Astana.

“But I think Central Asia was always skipped and overlooked,” he said. “We were only considered to be a natural-resources type play.”

Kakishev argues that Kazakhstan today offers more than resources. With access to Eurasian markets, investment incentives and special economic zones, he believes AIFC can serve as a platform for Chinese companies seeking international expansion.

Building a common-law financial center in Astana

AIFC was established as a financial center with its own legal and regulatory framework.

“We are set up as a common law jurisdiction,” Kakishev said.

The center has its own regulator, the Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA), as well as its own court and arbitration system. Its court includes English judges, with a former Chief Justice of England and Wales serving as chairman.

AIFC also operates the Astana International Exchange (AIX), which focuses on international currencies within the common-law framework, while Kazakhstan’s stock exchange in Almaty mainly handles tenge-denominated securities.

According to Kakishev, AIFC offers corporate structures including partnerships, private and public companies, foundations and trusts.

“We are quite business oriented,” he said, noting that AIFC can adjust regulations faster than national legislative processes.

AIFC had surpassed 6,200 registered companies at the time of the interview and provides an Expat Centre that Kakishev described as a “one-stop shop,” offering around 120 services including visa support.

From finance to AI infrastructure

As Chief Product Officer, Kakishev oversees new financial products and investment initiatives within AIFC.

One focus is aviation finance. Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan are expected to lease around 300 new aircraft over the next four years, and AIFC is developing a framework to attract aviation leasing companies while exploring sustainable aviation fuel.

The center is also expanding into green finance, renewable energy certificates and carbon markets. Kakishev said Kazakhstan’s large land area creates opportunities for nature-based projects.

Islamic finance is another area of development. “We have both Malaysian and Arabic scholars within our organization,” he said. “We came up with a framework which we believe actually reconciles both.”

AIFC is also examining Kazakhstan’s role in artificial intelligence. Kakishev said the country may not compete directly in large language models.

“We realized that Kazakhstan probably is too late on the large language models application,” he said.

Instead, he believes Kazakhstan could find opportunities in AI infrastructure. “We see a lot of potential for Kazakhstan to play in the infrastructure space, building data centers.”

Turning resources and ideas into investable opportunities

While mining remains central to Kazakhstan’s economy, AIFC is working to address financing gaps in the sector.

Kakishev pointed to a dual IPO with Hong Kong involving Jiaxin International Resources Investment Limited as an example. “We would like to have more Jiaxins,” he said.

AIFC is developing a junior mining platform where exploration companies can present projects to investors after preliminary assessments. “We are acting as a centralized depository for all junior mining opportunities,” Kakishev said.

The center is applying similar financial structures to creative industries, allowing filmmakers and musicians to establish investment vehicles through AIFC.

“For international players, it’s also easier to invest when there is a proper common-law GP-LP kind of structure,” he said.

China, Hong Kong and Kazakhstan’s next phase

For Kakishev, China and Hong Kong are natural partners in Kazakhstan’s development. “I think China, including Hong Kong, is a natural fit with the opportunities which exist in Kazakhstan,” he said.

He sees Hong Kong as a source of capital and financial expertise, while China can contribute manufacturing and technology capabilities. “The third dimension I would mention is the technology transfer,” Kakishev said. “We don’t want only investments; we want capabilities.”

He highlighted areas including automobile manufacturing, advanced manufacturing, composites and critical minerals. “We would like to use that capability and create a win-win situation for both of the countries,” he said.

Kazakhstan as a testing ground for startups

Kakishev also believes Kazakhstan could become a launchpad for Chinese technology companies expanding overseas. “Technology companies usually want to scale,” he said.

Rather than immediately entering highly competitive markets, startups could use Kazakhstan and Eurasia as a testing environment. “We think that Kazakhstan market, Eurasian market, in its own right, can be a good piloting stage,” Kakishev said.

“Kazakhstan was always at the crossroads, uniting Europe, China, north Russia, and some of the Arabic culture as well, because of the historical heritage,” he said.

“People here understand different cultures, and it’s a good place to test your hypotheses and pivot your startup into a new geographic location,” he said.

For Kakishev, China-Kazakhstan cooperation has two major tracks: government digitalization and startup ecosystem development. “I definitely believe there is both big partnerships, win-win, both in the government sector as well as the private sector,” he said.

For Chinese companies looking beyond traditional markets, Kazakhstan wants to be seen not only as a source of resources, but as a financial hub, technology partner and testing ground for global expansion.

Tesla has launched the refreshed Model Y Performance all-wheel-drive version in China at a starting price of RMB 369,000.

The Model Y Performance has a CLTC range of 659 kilometers, a top speed of 250 kph and a 0–100 kph time of 3.5 seconds. [IT Home, in Chinese]

The module combines 36 channels operating at 200 gigabits per second each. Near-package optics places optical components closer to switching chips, reducing signal loss and power consumption as AI clusters connect more processors. Huawei said the product is […]
item.content:encoded:
Huawei has showcased what it calls the industry’s first 7.2-terabit-per-second near-package optics (NPO) module for AI infrastructure.

The module combines 36 channels operating at 200 gigabits per second each. Near-package optics places optical components closer to switching chips, reducing signal loss and power consumption as AI clusters connect more processors. Huawei said the product is still in development and that volume production will depend on supply-chain and manufacturing readiness. [SCMP]

item.title: Alipay to launch an AI wallet agent for trusted AI payments
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Alipay plans to launch an AI wallet agent to help users manage AI payments as it shifts its focus from merely enabling transactions to making them trustworthy, the company said at the 2026 Bund Summit. The agent will support Vibe Pay, Skill Pay and Machine Pay, along with e-commerce functions such as recurring purchases, assisted […]
item.content:encoded:
Alipay plans to launch an AI wallet agent to help users manage AI payments as it shifts its focus from merely enabling transactions to making them trustworthy, the company said at the 2026 Bund Summit.

The agent will support Vibe Pay, Skill Pay and Machine Pay, along with e-commerce functions such as recurring purchases, assisted buying and assisted booking. It will be built on Ant Group’s APASS trust infrastructure and KYA framework, which cover an agent’s identity, intent, authorization and behavior. Alipay has also outlined its broader AI Pay and agent-payment infrastructure. [TechNode reporting]

item.title: Kazakhstan’s Venture Market Is Growing Up — and Looking to China
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Kazakhstan’s venture capital ecosystem is still young, but Askar Bilisbekov, CEO and board member of Alem Capital Management, sees room for growth through more institutional capital, stronger international links and deeper ties with China. “We’re still building our ecosystem,” Bilisbekov told TechNode in Astana. “Lots of missing parts in our ecosystem.” Those gaps include M&A […]
item.content:encoded:
Kazakhstan’s venture capital ecosystem is still young, but Askar Bilisbekov, CEO and board member of Alem Capital Management, sees room for growth through more institutional capital, stronger international links and deeper ties with China.

“We’re still building our ecosystem,” Bilisbekov told TechNode in Astana. “Lots of missing parts in our ecosystem.”

Those gaps include M&A and capital markets, while venture capital itself remains unfamiliar to many local investors. Still, Bilisbekov sees growing interest beyond Kazakhstan’s traditional oil and gas industries, including private equity, critical minerals and technology.

BUILDING CAPITAL — AND HELPING STARTUPS SCALE

Bilisbekov describes Alem Capital not simply as a fund, but as an “investment platform.” The government-backed initiative received its license in July 2025 and completed its first closing that October, raising $115 million across two funds: $95 million for venture capital and $20 million for crypto. Roughly two-thirds of its capital comes from the private sector.

“We started our deployment process officially” this year, Bilisbekov said.

Alem Capital has selected six funds across its first two cohorts and plans additional funds focused on energy alternatives and AI data centers, with a target size of $1 billion. Its mandate covers Kazakhstan, Central Asia, the Caucasus and global investments, although Kazakhstan remains the primary focus.

For Bilisbekov, the challenge is not simply a lack of money. “It’s not because we’re lacking in capital here; it’s more on the awareness of the asset class itself,” he said. “If you don’t know the asset class, you don’t invest there.”

But startups face another obstacle: scale. Kazakhstan and other former Soviet markets remain fragmented, Bilisbekov said. Local founders are expanding into the United States, Europe and Africa, but China remains less explored.

“Nobody is thinking that we can do an expanded opportunity in China,” he said.

“If we do cross-border development, founders coming from China here, and our founders going to China, I think that’s another opportunity to look into bigger opportunities to scale,” he said.

BUILDING A VC BRIDGE WITH CHINA

Alem Capital has organized an LP-GP Summit for two consecutive years, bringing international investors into Kazakhstan’s technology ecosystem, including Chinese VCs.

“I want to see them more,” Bilisbekov said. “Sharing the same borders and being close neighbors and allies, we have to expand our economic development in the space where I’m currently working: VC and private equity.”

He also sees opportunities for Chinese deep-tech companies because of Kazakhstan’s STEM talent, scientific institutions and laboratories.

“Of course, hundred percent,” Bilisbekov said when asked whether Chinese companies in robotics, AI hardware, batteries and energy could find opportunities in the country.

“I think that’s also a good foundation for any deep-tech startups or deep-tech projects to roll out their operations here in Kazakhstan.”

Why Kazakhstan could appeal to global investors

Bilisbekov puts political stability and neutrality at the top of Kazakhstan’s investment pitch.

“Kazakhstan’s number one thing is our political stability and our neutrality.”

He described the country as being “like a Switzerland in Asian markets,” citing its relationships with China, Russia, the United States, Europe and the United Kingdom. He also highlighted the Astana International Financial Centre and its independent court and common-law framework.

“Any investor wants to come to a country where his or her rights are protected,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s digitalization is another advantage. Bilisbekov said government services and financial transactions can increasingly be handled by phone, while internet coverage is close to 90%.

“I don’t bring any ID. I have everything on my phone,” he said. “You see, that’s the level of digitalization of our country.”

He also pointed to more than 5,000 startups, Astana Hub’s growing role, and sectors including fintech, agritech and spacetech. Robotics could also become important, with Bilisbekov expecting a “super cycle” driven by AI and robotics.

For Bilisbekov, however, the strongest case for Kazakhstan is made in person.

“Come to our country to see with your own eyes what kind of opportunities we have,” he said. “My opinion is the opinion of one person. You’re gonna find opinions of different people.”

Kazakhstan’s venture ecosystem is still developing, but Bilisbekov believes more capital, more founders and stronger international links — particularly with China — could help shape its next phase of growth.

item.title: China’s Humanoid Robot Boom, Part III: When is the ChatGPT moment for humanoid robots?
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter. The first time many people saw a humanoid robot, it was probably doing something impressive: dancing, flipping, or performing a carefully rehearsed routine. The industry’s biggest challenge now lies in turning those impressive demonstrations into robots that can perform useful tasks in everyday environments. […]
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

The first time many people saw a humanoid robot, it was probably doing something impressive: dancing, flipping, or performing a carefully rehearsed routine. The industry’s biggest challenge now lies in turning those impressive demonstrations into robots that can perform useful tasks in everyday environments.

That is the challenge facing China’s rapidly growing humanoid robot industry. As companies move from demonstrations toward commercial deployment, they are exploring how these machines can take on practical roles in workplaces, services and other real-world settings.

Chinese companies are moving faster and at greater scale than U.S. rivals at this stage, Selina Xu, China and AI policy lead in Eric Schmidt’s office, told TechCrunch. But when does the sector get its “ChatGPT moment” — the breakthrough Sam Altman says could be just a few years away?

The Story Behind China’s Dominance

Three forces are giving China an early edge: cost, capital and a large testing ground for commercialization. Its manufacturing base, reinforced by the EV supply chain for batteries, sensors and other components, lets robot makers source hardware locally, iterate faster and lower prices. In the first half of 2026, five Chinese companies accounted for 86% of global humanoid shipments, according to Counterpoint Research.

Funding is another factor. XPeng’s robotics unit raised more than $900 million in August, valuing it at more than $6.3 billion. Galbot raised RMB 2.5 billion ($362 million) in March after a $300 million-plus round in late 2025 valued it at about $3 billion.

China also offers a broad range of potential markets. Humanoids are being deployed or tested in automotive manufacturing, electronics, logistics, aerospace and energy. But commercialization remains early, with deployments ranging from purchases to preorders and pilots, while large-scale repeat orders remain limited.

The Hard Part of the Robot Boom

China’s humanoid makers still face questions over AI systems and integrated software. Vision-language-action models and world models remain early, while Nvidia leads with an end-to-end robotics software stack, leaving many Chinese startups reliant on its Orin chips even as domestic chipmakers develop alternatives.

The harder test is turning physical capability into sustainable commercial demand. Jiang Han, a senior researcher at the Pangoal Institution, told TechNode that repeat orders and customer payback periods are key signs that robots are solving real problems rather than simply attracting trial use. He said China’s longer-term advantage lies not in low manufacturing costs alone, but in combining supply-chain cost advantages with rapid hardware and algorithm iteration.

Data remains another bottleneck. Unlike large language models, robot developers cannot simply scrape the internet for examples of physical interaction. They are turning to synthetic data, simulation, reinforcement learning and real-world deployments. Harry Mellsop, co-founder of Antioch, a startup building simulation tools for physical AI, has described physical AI as being in its “GPT-2 era,” referring to the OpenAI model that predated ChatGPT, with more data and computing power still needed.

Reliability can break an otherwise impressive demo. Speaking at BEYOND Expo, Fu Sheng, chairman and CEO of Cheetah Mobile and chairman of service robotics company OrionStar, said robotics’ hardest challenge is “the last 1%”: a 99% success rate still means one failure in every 100 attempts. He argued that commercial robots must prove they can operate reliably and efficiently over long periods before they become useful workers.

Safety and security add another hurdle. A high-profile accident could trigger public backlash as deployment accelerates. Jiang also pointed to supply-chain vulnerabilities and data-security compliance as gaps Chinese robot makers still need to address, particularly in European and U.S. markets.

Useful First, General Later

Yuli Zhao, chief strategy officer at Galbot, a Chinese humanoid robotics startup that focuses on embodied intelligence and commercial deployment, expects demand to emerge first in manufacturing, warehouse logistics and retail, where tasks are repetitive and workflows are clear — conditions he said create real demand and give humanoid robots a better chance to deliver value at scale.

Fu makes a similar case for specialization. Rather than chasing a general-purpose robot, he argued that companies may find more commercial value in well-defined jobs such as agriculture, transport and sorting, then improve reliability, efficiency and deployment around those tasks.

But the longer-term goal remains general intelligence. Jiang said a true “ChatGPT moment” would require a general embodied-intelligence model that can understand natural-language instructions and break complex tasks into steps rather than rely on preprogrammed actions. The key bottleneck, he said, is handling long-tail situations in unstructured environments, where robots can still fail when something unfamiliar happens.

China may be well positioned to run that cycle quickly. Zhao described its advantage as “speed-to-scale,” with R&D, supply chains, manufacturing, integration and deployment operating in a tight loop — moving robots from prototypes into real-world use faster and feeding operational data into the next round of development.
